source: Consensus is Not Verification (2026) arXiv 2603.06612, accuracy tables at T=1.0
finding: Across 19 (benchmark, model) cells SP beat direct majority in 9, lost in 9 and tied in 1; no consistent gain. Com2Sense is the extreme: majority far below single-sample.
limits: Item counts of 35 to 100 give wide CIs; most SP-minus-majority gaps are inside noise. Com2Sense shows SP can partly rescue a bad majority (+4 to +6) yet still be far below one sample. Win/loss tally is my count from the table rows (HLE, BoolQ, PtF, Com2Sense; Gemma missing on Com2Sense).
agent_relevance: At equal samples, SP did not reliably beat majority with 2025-era open models. Do not adopt SP as a default selector.

source: Consensus is Not Verification (2026) arXiv 2603.06612, protocol
finding: Protocol: 5 models (Gemma-3-4B, GPT-oss-20B/120B, Qwen3-32B/235B), 25 samples per model at each T in {0.7,1.0}; inter-model crowd of 125 votes. Reasoning/thinking mode is not stated.
numbers: Four benchmarks (HLE binary 35, BoolQ 100, Com2Sense 100, Predict-the-Future 100) plus a random-string control of 10,000 prompts; MATH and AIME 128 problems each with 200 samples. Plurality flips in 2.9% of 1,575 (question, model) pairs between T=0.7 and 1.0. Abstract says five benchmarks, body describes four plus control; Appendix B (50 per cell) does not obviously match 25 per temperature.
limits: Gap 10 stays partly open: no larger item sets and no stated reasoning-mode test; the paper itself calls the forecasting set small.
agent_relevance: Our own test must log reasoning mode, sample count and item count, and use at least several hundred items.

source: Consensus is Not Verification (2026) arXiv 2603.06612, Appendix D prediction prompt
finding: SP here uses verbalised meta-prediction: each sample says its own answer and the percent of other models that will say YES. SP picks the answer whose observed share beats the mean predicted share.
numbers: Prompt: 'What percentage of language models will answer YES ... YES:XX NO:XX'. Parsing regex YES:?\s*(\d+); missing values default to 0.5. The paper says predictions 'correlate strongly with vote shares' (Fig. 6) but gives no correlation coefficient.
limits: Gap 5 only partly answered: predictions track the vote share, which suggests they mostly echo the model's own consensus; no test of signal beyond own vote.
agent_relevance: Cheap to copy: one extra line in the sample output. Measure the correlation of predicted share with the sample's own answer to see if it adds information.

source: Consensus is Not Verification (2026) arXiv 2603.06612, MATH and AIME error concentration
finding: When a plurality is wrong, one wrong answer usually dominates the errors. That is the shared-error case where SP cannot help.
numbers: MATH: plurality-wrong rate 3.9 to 25.8%; most common wrong answer is 65 to 87% of wrong responses; on 53% of questions where several models err they converge on the same wrong answer. AIME: plurality-wrong 3.9 to 75.8%, concentration 20 to 63%. Random-string control: inter-model correlation up to 0.35. Inverse-SP about 80% on HLE but chance elsewhere.
limits: Concentration is measured across models; within-one-model samples likely correlate even more (my inference).
agent_relevance: For gap 2: measure the top-wrong-answer share of our scaffold's wrong samples; if above about 60%, expect SP to add little.

source: Consensus is Not Verification (2026) arXiv 2603.06612, Section 5.3 limitations
finding: Authors say verbalised confidence tracks consensus almost as strongly as correctness, and that temperature and ensembling change surface form more than beliefs. Pooling 5 models across 3 families did not restore independence. No persona test.
numbers: 125 votes per question in the pooled crowd; no persona or prompt-diversity arm. Calibration (ECE) is not reported here.
limits: Supports gap 7 answer 'model mixing alone is not enough'; says nothing positive about personas because they were not tried. Gap 8 gets no new support.
agent_relevance: Persona/model diversity is untested for SP; do not assume it fixes independence.

source: Ai, Pan, Simchi-Levi, Tambe, Xu (2025/2026) Beyond Majority Voting, simulation with K options
finding: Simulated agents (accuracy 0.6 to 0.9): plain SP is below majority at every K; ISP and the optimal rule are above, but the ISP edge shrinks as K grows (order 1/K).
limits: Simulation with conditionally independent agents of fixed known accuracy; real LLMs violate that. Open-ended answers are not handled (listed as future work, no clustering).
agent_relevance: Gap 9: with 4 or more options plain SP is a weak selector; gains of any higher-order rule are small.

source: Ai et al. (2025/2026) Beyond Majority Voting, real-LLM results and failures
finding: Real ensembles: ISP and weighted rules beat majority by small margins; ISP was the top method in only 12.5% of 16 ensembles. The best single model can beat every aggregator. The weighted rule (OW) gives the big gain on hard items.
numbers: Data sizes: UltraFeedback 56,380 kept of 63,135; MMLU 109,820 of 115,700; ARMMAN 11,785 of 12,000. MMLU: MV 89.32, ISP 90.01, OW 90.37, single best 91.02. Eight models: MV 87.19, ISP 87.92, OW-I 88.64. MMLU-hard (13,886 Q): MV 17.23, ISP 18.66, OW 24.79. Table 10 wins/losses vs MV: UltraFeedback 2,545/1,727 (t 12.53); MMLU 1,821/659; ARMMAN 264/195. Failures (ARMMAN): ISP 68.82 vs MV 69.06; OW-I 68.53 vs MV 70.10.
limits: One answer per model per question (no repeated sampling); token cost not compared. Large N makes tiny gaps significant.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 closed in direction: use higher-order information as a weight (OW) rather than as an SP selector. Cost-matched value still untested.

source: Ai et al. (2025/2026) Beyond Majority Voting, Appendix C correlated agents
finding: Theory: if question difficulty varies, independence given the label fails at population level, but ISP still has expected advantage at least that of majority, which is at least that of SP. Stress tests with correlated ensembles keep ISP and OW above majority.
numbers: Theorem C.3: E[Adv_ISP] >= E[Adv_MV] >= E[Adv_SP]. Tables 11-13: largest gain 7.7 points (OW-I 83.97 vs MV 76.27, ARMMAN, correlated set).
limits: Gap 2 partly closed: no numeric correlation threshold is given; the result is an ordering, not a cutoff.
agent_relevance: Plain SP ranks below majority under difficulty-driven correlation; this matches the Consensus paper.

source: Ai et al. (2025/2026) Beyond Majority Voting, how second-order information is obtained
finding: No model was asked to predict others. Second-order data are co-occurrence counts of answers across models, estimated from the same votes. Prompts ask only for the letter.
numbers: P-hat(A_i=s_k | A_j=s_l) = count(A_i=s_k, A_j=s_l) / count(A_j=s_l). Position bias checked only on ARMMAN (GPT-4o 49.7% A, Qwen 51.4% A).
limits: Not a test of verbalised meta-prediction (gap 5 stays open for ISP). It estimates the signal from agreement patterns, which costs no extra tokens.
agent_relevance: A free alternative to asking for predicted shares: use co-occurrence of our own samples' answers.

source: Kim, Garg, Peng, Garg (2025) Correlated Errors in Large Language Models, ICML
finding: Across over 350 LLMs, models agree on a wrong answer far more than chance. Larger, more accurate models are more correlated, even across providers. Diversity by model name is weak.
numbers: HuggingFace 349 models, 12,032 questions: mean agreement when both wrong 0.423 vs about 0.12 by chance; 100% of pairs above chance. HELM 71 models, 14,042 Q: 0.60 vs 1/3; 97.5% above. Same company +0.066 (HF) and +0.022 (HELM); same architecture +0.076. Both-accurate interaction +0.023 to +0.043. R-squared 0.34 to 0.61. Resumes: 20 models, 1,800 pairs.
limits: Does not test voting or SP. Agreement is pairwise across models, not across samples of one model.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: if different frontier models already agree on wrong answers about half the time, same-model samples correlate at least as much (inference). SP's independence assumption is unlikely to hold for our scaffold.

source: Aitchison, Jeen, Shevlane, Day (2026) Diversity is the Strength of the AI Crowd, arXiv 2606.29661
finding: For a fixed forecast budget, the best mix pairs accurate models with less-correlated ones. Grok 4 adds most because its errors are least like the others. Only weighted averaging was used, not SP.
numbers: 113 binary Metaculus questions, 5 forecasters, R=3 samples each, budget B=5. Best allocation: 2 x FT-gpt-oss-120b, 1 each Gemini 3 Pro, GPT-5, Grok 4. Weights 0.56/0.26/0.18. Replaceability of Grok 4 about 1.7 points. Error similarity by Jensen-Shannon divergence; numbers only in an unreadable figure.
limits: Gap 7: model diversity helps weighted averages, but no persona arm and no SP arm. Page read via a summary; numeric JS values not available.
agent_relevance: If we use a crowd, spend samples on a different model or prompt family, not more samples of the same one.

source: Goel et al. (2023, v2) On the Truthfulness of Surprisingly Likely Responses of LLMs, arXiv 2311.07692
finding: Scoring each candidate by P(r|question) / P(r|'?') beats picking the most probable one on TruthfulQA for base models of all sizes. The prior is the model's own probability with the question removed.
numbers: TruthfulQA 817 Q, 3 to 25 candidates (mean 7.6). MaxPost vs MaxRatio: GPT-2 XL 0.36 vs 0.52; LLaMA-2 7B 0.34 vs 0.58; 13B 0.43 vs 0.59; 70B (4-bit) 0.37 vs 0.58. Text says +24 for 70B; table gives +21 (+24 is the 7B row). COPA dev 500 and StoryCloze dev 1,871 also tested.
limits: Base models only, no chat or reasoning models; works over a fixed candidate list, not open generation. This is a likelihood-ratio idea, not a poll.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: supports multi-option scoring when candidates are given. Cheap to try as a tie-break among candidate answers.

source: Han, Schoenebeck, Tao, Xia (2025) The Art of Two-Round Voting, arXiv 2505.10377
finding: SP is a special case of a two-round equilibrium (vote, see tally, vote again with a threshold). LLM agents in a hiring simulation: DeepSeek R1 gained from two rounds under biased signals, GPT-4o did not.
numbers: n=40 agents, 50 runs per cell, prior 0.5. Informed-majority rate: R1 one-round 0.56 / two-round 0.88 (accurate description), 0.52 / 0.78 (vague); GPT-4o 0.50 / 0.48 and 0.52 / 0.50; unbiased signals all 1.00.
limits: Simulated role-play voters with assigned signals, not factual questions. Gain depends on the model. Only first 100k characters read.
agent_relevance: Showing the first-round tally to a second pass is another route to the SP effect; model-dependent.

source: Large Language Models Systematically Favor Popular Options (2026) arXiv 2608.29257
finding: Models pick popular wrong options. In the hardest PopMCQ setting (all distractors more popular than the answer) they choose a popular wrong answer 66% of the time. A label-free correction (PopDebias) raises accuracy up to 54.1 points on 22 open models.
numbers: 22 open-source models, 0.5B to 32B; six popularity strategies.
limits: Abstract only; the link to SP is my inference, not a result in the paper.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 (indirect): shared popular misconceptions are the case SP is meant to rescue, yet models lean toward the popular answer, so their predicted shares may be inflated for it too.

source: Wang et al. (2022) Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning, arXiv 2203.11171
finding: Baseline for gap 1: majority over sampled reasoning paths gives large gains over greedy chain of thought on older models.
numbers: Gains over greedy CoT: GSM8K +17.9, AQuA +12.2, SVAMP +11.0, StrategyQA +6.4, ARC-challenge +3.9 points.
limits: Abstract only; 2022 models. Any SP gain must be measured on top of this much larger majority gain; the 0.5 to 1.5 point gains in d07 are small by comparison.
agent_relevance: Majority/self-consistency is the arm SP has to beat at equal tokens; no published test of that with a current reasoning model was found.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd, arXiv 2402.19379
finding: A crowd of 12 LLMs aggregated on 31 binary forecasting questions was not statistically different from 925 human forecasters. Simple averaging of human and machine forecasts beat feeding the human median to the model.
numbers: Study 2: exposure to the median human forecast improved GPT-4 and Claude 2 accuracy by 17 to 28%.
limits: Abstract only. Plain aggregation, no SP or meta-prediction.
agent_relevance: Model-mixture crowds can work without SP; supports diversity over cleverer selectors.

source: Hosseini, Mandal, Shah, Shi (2021) Surprisingly Popular Voting Recovers Rankings, Surprisingly!, IJCAI (PDF text read)
finding: Ranking version of SP is tested on three ground-truth datasets (230 countries by population, 15,743 movies by box office, 80 paintings by auction price) and compared with plurality, runoff and other rules.
numbers: Datasets: geography 230 countries, movies 15,743, paintings 80. SP parameters learned on a train split.
limits: Extension of SP to rankings, not an independent replication of the 21.3% claim. I did not read the result tables closely.
agent_relevance: Partial support for gap 9 (multi-option): SP works for rankings when predictions are available.

source: Amiri-Margavi et al. (2025) Enhancing Answer Reliability Through Inter-Model Consensus, arXiv 2411.16797
finding: Four models (GPT-4, Llama-3-70B, Claude-3-Opus, Gemini-1.5-Flash) generating and answering PhD-level statistics questions; authors say collaboration raises reliability. Abstract gives no numbers and does not compare diverse with same-model groups.
limits: Weak evidence for gap 7; the diversity conclusion is an inference.
agent_relevance: Do not cite as support for persona or model diversity.

source: Search note: independent replication of Prelec et al. 2017 (gap 6)
finding: A web search for replications or failed replications returned only the original paper, press coverage and the Hosseini ranking paper. No same-design large replication was found. arXiv, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar APIs returned rate-limit errors in this run, and a second web search was refused for budget, so the search was incomplete.
numbers: Known independent field tests remain Lee et al. 2018 (256 games, SP 68%) and Rutchick et al. 2020 (SP worst in football, small gains elsewhere).
limits: Absence of evidence under a rate-limited search, not proof. Palley and Soll (403), the Nature page (login redirect) and ResearchGate (403) could not be opened.
agent_relevance: Treat the 21.3% as a single-study result.
